claim_traces.claim_title: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood
claim_traces.claim_text: "Octopuses have three hearts and their blood is blue."
reasoning_steps: Octopuses have three hearts: two branchial hearts that pump blood through the gills to receive oxygen, and one systemic heart that pumps the oxygenated blood throughout the rest of the body
Their blood is blue because it uses a copper-rich protein called hemocyanin to transport oxygen, unlike the iron-based hemoglobin found in human and mammalian red blood cells.

claim_traces.claim_title: Lightning never strikes the same place twice
claim_traces.claim_text: "Lightning never strikes the same place twice."
reasoning_steps: The claim that "lightning never strikes the same place twice" is a common myth that is scientifically false
According to the National Weather Service (NWS) and atmospheric scientists, lightning frequently hits the same location multiple times, particularly tall, pointed, or isolated conductive structures
For example, the Empire State Building in New York City is struck by lightning an average of 20 to 25 times every year
Additionally, individual lightning flashes can consist of multiple channel discharges hitting the exact same ground location in rapid succession during a single storm event.

claim_traces.claim_title: The Moon is drifting away from Earth
claim_traces.claim_text: "The Moon is slowly moving away from Earth at a rate of about 3.8 centimeters per year."
reasoning_steps: Data from the Lunar Laser Ranging experiment—which uses retroreflectors left on the lunar surface during Apollo missions—has precisely measured the rate at which the Moon is receding from Earth
The Moon moves away from Earth at approximately 3.8 centimeters (about 1.5 inches) per year

This phenomenon is driven by tidal interactions: gravitational forces create tidal bulges in Earth's oceans, and the gravitational pull of these bulges transfers rotational energy and angular momentum from Earth to the Moon, boosting it into a higher orbit.
